title: The Tool and the Hand
text:
Essay, October 2026. A short, personal essay. Both figures are schematics of my own, drawn with figs.py; they show a shape, not measured data.
In short. AI raises the ceiling of what one person can do. It does not move the floor each of us stands on. Productivity is not a property of tools but of the relationship between a person and their work: curiosity, ownership, the habit of finishing. A person who postponed before will postpone with AI, only faster. The tool multiplies what is already there, so the gap between people who know why they work and those still waiting to be told will widen. A mindset can change, but through people, not software.

title: The Tool and the Hand
text:
1. The oldest promise
Every new tool arrives with a promise. The printing press would make us wiser. The telephone would bring us closer. The spreadsheet would free the accountant, and the internet would put all knowledge within reach of everyone. Each of these tools delivered something real. None of them delivered the person.
Artificial intelligence arrives carrying the largest promise of all: that anyone, with the right question, can now write, code, analyse and decide faster and better than ever before. And it is true that the ceiling has risen. What has not moved is the floor each of us stands on.

title: The Tool and the Hand
section: 2. The tool amplifies; it does not transform
text:
2. The tool amplifies; it does not transform
A tool extends a hand. It does not give that hand an intention. Put a powerful engine in a car whose driver does not know where to go, and you get more horsepower spent idling at the same crossroads.
Productivity is not a property of tools. It is a property of the relationship between a person and their work: curiosity, ownership, the habit of finishing what was started, the courage to show something imperfect and improve it quickly. These are not features you can install.
So the person who used to postpone will now postpone with AI. The one who waited for perfect instructions will now wait for the perfect prompt. The one who avoided hard thinking will find in AI an excellent accomplice for avoiding it, and the result will look polished, which makes it more dangerous, not less. Hesitation, multiplied, is just faster hesitation.

AI multiplies what is already there. It does not supply what is missing.

Meanwhile, the person who was already driven, who asked questions, tried, failed and tried again, will move remarkably further (Figure 1). The real risk of this new tool is not that it replaces people. It is that it quietly widens the gap between those who know why they work and those who are still waiting to be told.



Figure 1. The same tool, three mindsets. AI lifts each person in proportion to what they already bring, so the gap between them grows. Schematic, my own.

title: The Tool and the Hand
section: 3. A mindset is shaped, not installed
text:
3. A mindset is shaped, not installed
This is not a judgement on the slow. Few people are born indifferent; many were simply never shown another way. Nobody gave them responsibility, nobody trusted them with an unfinished idea, nobody celebrated a small step forward. A mindset is not a fixed trait. It is the sediment of the examples we saw, the feedback we received, and the freedom we were or were not given.
That is why it can change, but not through software. It changes through people (Figure 2). A manager who explains the why before the how. A colleague who shares a half-finished draft without shame. A team where asking a question is a sign of engagement rather than weakness. Small wins, repeated, until finishing becomes a habit and initiative feels natural. This work is slow, human and unglamorous. No licence can buy it, and no rollout plan can schedule it.



Figure 2. How a mindset is shaped. Each turn of the loop is made by people. AI can speed up a loop that is already turning, but it cannot start one. Schematic, my own.

title: The Tool and the Hand
text:
4. The question to ask first
Before asking “how do we deploy AI?”, an organisation, or a person, might ask a simpler and more uncomfortable question: what exactly are we about to amplify? If the answer is curiosity, ownership and a taste for doing things well, the tool will be a marvel. If the answer is waiting, fear of being wrong and a lack of purpose, the tool will change nothing except the speed at which we stand still.
The hammer did not build the cathedral. People did: people who knew why they were cutting stone. The tools have never been as powerful as they are today. It has never mattered more to tend to the hand that holds them.



Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.

title: What Survives Comparison
text:
After Nothing From Outside, Everything From Inside, a reader sent me a question I could not stop thinking about:

If two observers inside the same closed universe each keep their own records, do they always end up agreeing on one world?

My first answer was one word: no. That was true, but too short. “No” sounds like the two observers live in different worlds and that is the end of it. What I actually believe fits in one sentence: agreement is always agreement for someone. It exists for whoever holds both records and can compare them. It does not exist anywhere else.
In the last essay one observer came in to rescue the universe from having only one state. This essay puts in two, and follows that sentence through three cases. I am still not a physicist. This is still curiosity.

title: What Survives Comparison
text:
After Nothing From Outside, Everything From Inside, a reader sent me a question I could not stop thinking about:

If two observers inside the same closed universe each keep their own records, do they always end up agreeing on one world?

My first answer was one word: no. That was true, but too short. “No” sounds like the two observers live in different worlds and that is the end of it. What I actually believe fits in one sentence: agreement is always agreement for someone. It exists for whoever holds both records and can compare them. It does not exist anywhere else.
In the last essay one observer came in to rescue the universe from having only one state. This essay puts in two, and follows that sentence through three cases. I am still not a physicist. This is still curiosity.

title: What Survives Comparison
text:
Nobody holds the master copy
The ordinary picture goes like this. There is one world, out there. Each observer takes notes on it. If two observers disagree, at least one made a mistake, and you can find out who by checking against the world.
In a closed universe that last step has nowhere to happen. There is no outside, so there is no referee holding the master copy. The previous essay said that the view from nowhere returns one state, which is to say nothing. So the world cannot be what guarantees agreement. Any agreement has to be produced from inside, by the observers themselves.
That is the real reason for my “no”. Not that observers must disagree, but that nothing is there to make them agree in advance.
The physicists who brought the observer back saw this coming. Harlow, Usatyuk and Zhao also consider two observers: each can treat the other as just more matter, and the rules require the two accounts to fit together. Agreement is not handed out by the universe. It is a condition the rules have to be built to satisfy, and the rules themselves are not settled yet.

title: What Survives Comparison
text:
Two observers, two pictures
The first way two records can differ came from the last essay. A bigger observer, one that can hold more, sees a richer universe. A smaller one sees a blurrier one.
Lay one record over the other, pixel by pixel, and they disagree almost everywhere. But that is the wrong comparison. The small observer simply did not record the fine detail. On what it did record, the large-scale shapes, the two agree.



Figure 1. Two observers, two pictures. The same toy universe as in the previous essay, recorded by a small observer and a large one. Laid over each other, the records differ almost everywhere (right). Read the large record at the small one’s scale and it matches the small record exactly. Below: disagreement against the size of the smaller observer, compared naively (red) and at the coarser scale (blue). In this toy the blue line is zero by construction; the point is what “agree” has to mean. The code is in figs.py.


So “do they agree?” only has a meaning on the questions both of them can ask. A blurry record and a sharp record do not contradict each other. One is just shorter.
Recent work suggests the differences can go further than blur. In 2024, De Vuyst, Eccles, Höhn and Kirklin showed that in quantum gravity even the entropy of a region, how much it can hide, depends on which observer describes it. Some quantities that looked like properties of the region turn out to belong to the region and the observer together.

title: What Survives Comparison
text:
When records meet
The second case is where quantum mechanics comes in.
Eugene Wigner imagined it in 1961. A friend sits in a sealed laboratory and measures an electron: up or down. She writes down the result. Wigner stands outside. As long as nothing leaks out, quantum mechanics tells Wigner to describe the whole lab, friend and notebook included, as still in a superposition of “saw up” and “saw down.” The friend has one result. Wigner has a description with both. Two observers, two accounts, and for now neither is wrong.
Since 2018 this has become sharper. Extended versions with two friends and two Wigners show that if every observer treats the others’ conclusions as facts, they reach a contradiction. In 2020 a team led by Kok-Wei Bong tested one such version, called Local Friendliness, in a real experiment. Its conclusion: you cannot keep all of these at once, that observed events are facts for everyone, that no influence travels faster than light, and that experimenters choose their settings freely. The “friends” in that experiment were simple photonic systems, so in 2023 Wiseman, Cavalcanti and Rieffel proposed a version where the friend can reason: an artificial intelligence running on a large quantum computer. Nobody can build it yet.
So quantum mechanics does not promise that one observer’s record is a fact for every other observer. That is the “no” again.
But look at what happens when Wigner opens the door and asks his friend what she saw. Now the two records interact, and quantum mechanics is firm about this case. Measure an electron, measure it again right away: same answer. Ask the friend, and her answer matches her notebook. There is one condition, and it is the heart of the paradoxes: while the lab is sealed, Wigner could in principle undo the friend’s observation, record included. The records whose truth is in doubt are the ones that never meet anything else, or are erased before they can. Records that are kept and brought together agree.
Rovelli’s relational quantum mechanics, which I mentioned last time, makes this a principle. In 2023 Adlam and Rovelli added a rule they call cross-perspective links: when one observer checks another’s record, what they find matches what the other recorded. Consistency is not a property of the world seen from above. It is a rule about meetings. The rule is debated, and so is relational quantum mechanics itself. But whichever view wins, agreement has to come from something that happens between observers.
That is what I meant in my reply. Two observers can tell different stories while apart. When they meet and compare, and their records have survived until then, quantum mechanics makes the stories fit. The agreement exists for them, at the meeting.

title: What Survives Comparison
section: Why so many people agree so easily
text:
Why so many people agree so easily
There is an obvious objection. You and I can both look at the Moon from different continents, never talk, and still agree on where it is. Why does agreement feel automatic?
Wojciech Zurek’s answer is called quantum Darwinism. The Moon is hit by sunlight, and each photon that bounces off carries away a tiny copy of where it is. There are astronomical numbers of these copies: Riedel and Zurek estimated that a speck of dust one micrometre across, in sunlight for one microsecond, has its position copied roughly a hundred million times. You catch some copies; I catch others. We never touch the Moon or each other, but we have read different copies of the same record.
The striking part is how few copies you need. In the toy below, one bit is copied, imperfectly, into sixty small pieces of environment. Read a few percent and you already know the whole bit. Read more and you learn nothing new, until you hold almost all of it. That flat stretch, the plateau, is why the world looks objective: many observers, each with a small and different fraction, land on the same answer.



Figure 2. Copies everywhere. Left: a system S scatters photons; observers A and B each catch a few different ones and never interact with S or with each other. Right: how much a fraction of the environment knows about S, for weak, medium and good copies, in an exact toy model with sixty pieces of environment. With good copies, 10% is enough to know the full bit; so is a different 10%. The second bit, a quantum correlation, needs almost the whole environment. The code is in figs.py.


Zurek chose the word Darwinism on purpose. Only some properties survive being copied over and over without being disturbed, and those become shared, the same for everyone. The rest stay private, or are lost. Parts of this have since been proved in general and seen in the lab, with photons and with spins in diamond. It does not explain why there is one result rather than another, only why everyone sees the same one.
This is very close to the sentence I wrote in my reply before I knew the theory: reality is not what is out there, but what survives comparison. Zurek would say what survives copying. But copying is comparison done in advance, by the environment, on everyone’s behalf. It is still agreement for someone. There are just a great many someones.

title: What Survives Comparison
text:
Behind each other’s horizons
The third case is the strangest, and it is where my “no” becomes something else.
Our universe is expanding faster and faster, so it has a horizon, a little like a black hole turned inside out. If dark energy stays constant, light that a distant galaxy emits today will never reach us, however long we wait. In empty de Sitter space, the universe from the previous essay, every observer sits at the centre of their own horizon.
Take two observers beyond each other’s horizon, A and C. Neither can ever send the other a message. They can both see light from a shared distant past, so they may hold records of the same old events. But they can never bring those records together.



Figure 3. Who can ever compare. A de Sitter universe drawn as a Penrose diagram: time goes up, light travels at 45 degrees, and the dashed red lines are horizons. Blue is everything A can ever see, amber everything C can ever see; they share a common past at the bottom. A and B stay close and can exchange records: when they compare, they are consistent. A and C never can. A third observer D, between them, can catch an early message from each and compare them, but can never send the result back to either. Schematic, my own; the code is in figs.py.


Do A and C agree on one world? For A and C themselves, the question has no answer. Not an unknown answer: no answer at all. Nothing either of them could ever do would settle it.
The diagram shows one subtlety. A third observer, D, between them, could catch an early message from each and compare them. But D could never tell A or C the result. So agreement between A and C may exist, but only for D. This is the opening sentence in its plainest form.
Physicists have met this before. In 1993 Susskind, Thorlacius and Uglum proposed black hole complementarity: someone who falls in and someone who stays out describe the horizon in incompatible ways, and both are right, because no one can ever hold both accounts. The idea was badly shaken by the firewall argument of 2012 and reshaped by the black-hole information results since 2019. In a form many physicists accept, its core survived: inside and outside are different encodings of the same thing, and no single observer can play them against each other.
In 2025 the same idea reached closed universes. Engelhardt, Gesteau and Harlow applied the new observer rules to a closed universe entangled with a pair of anti-de Sitter universes, the kind holography describes well, and called the result observer complementarity. An outside observer can run a test that says, in effect, there is no closed universe at all. An observer inside has their own consistent description of it. Here there is no D: nobody anywhere can receive messages from both. The result is contested: Antonini and collaborators (2025) and Higginbotham (2026) argued that the outside observer’s test cannot rule the closed universe out. But the debate is the reader’s question, now in the research literature.
So there is a kind of protection. Contradictions are allowed, but only where nobody can catch them.

title: What Survives Comparison
text:
One world, built
Put the three cases together.

Different sizes: their records differ, but on what both can see, they match.
When they meet: quantum mechanics makes their records consistent, and the environment often does the meeting for them.
Behind each other’s horizons: they can never compare, so for them “do they agree?” has no answer. At most a third observer holds it, and keeps it.

Nowhere in this list does the universe hand out one shared world from the start. One world is not given. It is what records build when they meet. It reaches exactly as far as meetings can reach, and it exists for whoever is at the meeting.
This also fits the grains from the last essay. A grain that pinches off into its own closed universe counts as one state from outside, and is everything to those inside. Now I see why the two descriptions never clash: once the grain has pinched off, nobody inside and nobody outside can ever compare notes, and there is no third place from which anyone could. The horizon that hides the grain also keeps both stories true. I did not know, when I wrote the last essay, that Engelhardt, Gesteau and Harlow had found something very close to this. I find that encouraging, and also a reason to be careful: their result is barely a year old and already disputed.

title: What Survives Comparison
section: A short echo in the usual subject
text:
A short echo in the usual subject
This blog is usually about AI, so one short echo, as an analogy only. Ask two AI models the same question and they may answer differently. There is no master copy of the right answer inside either. What I trust is what survives comparison: answers checked against each other, against a test, against a shared source. Agreement between machines, like agreement between observers, is not stored somewhere. It is built, for someone, where records meet.
The echo also runs the other way. The most demanding Wigner’s friend experiment proposed so far needs a friend that can reason, and the candidate is an AI on a quantum computer. One day “do two observers agree?” may be tested with a machine in the friend’s seat.

title: What Survives Comparison
text:
What I am not claiming

Wigner’s friend, the extended versions (Frauchiger and Renner, 2018) and the Local Friendliness results are about quantum mechanics without gravity. Applying them to observers in a closed universe is my own step.
The extended Wigner’s friend results are still argued over. Different interpretations escape the contradiction in different ways; I have described the relational way because it fits these essays, not because it is settled. Relational quantum mechanics itself is under serious criticism.
The cross-perspective links rule is a postulate added to relational quantum mechanics, not something derived from it. Lawrence, Markiewicz and Żukowski argue that relative facts are incompatible with quantum theory; Cavalcanti, Di Biagio and Rovelli replied, and the exchange continued in 2025.
The rules for including observers in quantum gravity are recent and not unique: Abdalla, Antonini, Iliesiu and Levine proposed different rules, and the two proposals disagree on the number of states. Most of these results use simplified models, often gravity in two dimensions.
Black hole complementarity in its 1993 form did not survive the firewall debate unchanged. Among the replies, Harlow and Hayden argued that catching the contradiction would need a computation longer than the black hole’s life; from 2019, Penington and Almheiri, Engelhardt, Marolf and Maxfield showed, mostly in simplified models, how information leaves an evaporating black hole. I use complementarity as an example of the idea, not as established physics. Observer complementarity for closed universes is a 2025 proposal and is contested.
Whether our own universe has a permanent horizon depends on how dark energy behaves in the far future. Since 2024 the DESI survey has found hints that it may be weakening; if it fades enough, the horizon could eventually stop being one. The hints are not conclusive.
Quantum Darwinism explains why observers agree on an outcome, not why there is one outcome. Its general result (Brandão, Piani and Horodecki, 2015) is about which question observers can ask; agreement on the answer needs the redundancy, which depends on the model. The toy in Figure 2 is a textbook model with perfect symmetry; real environments are messier, though the plateau has been found in more realistic models and in experiments.
The connection to the grains is speculation built on speculation.


Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.

title: Where Memory Lives
text:
An experiment, October 2026. Every number in Experiments 1 to 4 comes from sim.py, plain NumPy on a 4-core cloud CPU, with results in results.json and figures from figs.py. Other people’s numbers are cited where they appear. The networks are deliberately tiny: they test the shape of an argument, not any product. This essay puts to the test two ideas from Fast AI and An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle: bandwidth, and memory outside the weights.
In short. A language model keeps what it knows in four places: its weights, its working memory (the KV cache), whatever it can look up, and the habits it has compiled. Each is paid for at a different moment, and for a small model on a laptop that decides the design. Four experiments led me to one rule: keep in the weights what is used on every token; look up everything else, and keep what you look up short.

title: Where Memory Lives
text:
1. The question
Debates about small language models usually ask how much of a large model fits on a laptop. That treats a model as one block of knowledge to compress. I think the better question is what should live where?
Generating a token on a laptop is limited by memory bandwidth, not arithmetic: the machine reads every weight, and the whole cache of the conversation, for every token (Alizadeh et al. 2023). So where knowledge lives decides what it costs.



Figure 1. Schematic, my own. Four memories of a language model, ordered by how often you pay for them.

title: Where Memory Lives
section: 2. Experiment 1: how many facts fit in the weights

title: Where Memory Lives
text:
3. Experiment 2: changing one’s mind
Setup. A network of 18,752 parameters learned 1,500 facts perfectly. Then 75 facts changed and 75 new ones appeared. I updated it in two ways, each over 4 learning rates and 3 training lengths: fine-tuning on the 150 edits only, or rehearsing everything, all 1,575 facts. An external table got the same edits: overwrite 75 rows, add 75.



Figure 3. Experiment 2, measured. Left: each of the 24 fine-tuning runs, by the share of edits learned and of the other 1,425 facts kept; larger markers trained longer. Right: the worse of the two shares against training examples processed.


Result. Fine-tuning on the edits alone never got both right. The runs that learned 97% or more of the edits kept only 28% to 35% of the other facts; the best compromise kept 48% and learned 47%. Rehearsing everything got both to 100%, after 630,000 training examples, a cost that grows with everything the network knows. The table needed 150 writes and 0.04 ms.
Catastrophic interference is not new (McCloskey and Cohen 1989), and editing methods such as ROME and MEMIT do far better than plain fine-tuning (Meng et al. 2022, 2023), though models still degrade as edits accumulate (Gupta et al. 2024). The point is the contrast: in a table, an edit is local by construction; in weights, every fact shares every parameter. Contacts change, prices change, a client asks you to delete their data. A memory you can overwrite row by row is one you can keep true.

title: Where Memory Lives
text:
4. Experiment 3: looking it up
Setup. I stored ten thousand to four million facts as unit vectors of 256 numbers, clustered around 2,000 topics as real embeddings are. A question is a stored key plus noise, a paraphrase. Exact search compares it with every key, which takes O(Nd) operations: N keys of d = 256 numbers each (O(\cdot) means “grows in proportion to”). An inverted-file index (IVF) groups the keys into c = 4\sqrt{N} clusters once, then compares a question with the c cluster centres and with the keys of the p nearest clusters only. That takes O\big((c + pN/c)\,d\big) operations: c centres, plus p clusters of about N/c keys each. With c = 4\sqrt{N}, both terms grow like \sqrt{N}, so a memory a hundred times larger costs only ten times more per question (Douze et al. 2024).



Figure 4. Experiment 3, measured. Left: time per easy question against facts in memory. Right: one million facts at five noise levels; each line probes 1, 4, 16 and 64 clusters, and the star is exact search.


Result. Exact search took 29 ms over a million facts and 100 ms over four million. Probing 4 clusters took 0.25 and 0.5 ms, reading 5 and 11 MB. On harder questions, one cluster missed 5% to 20%, while four clusters matched exact search (95.5% against 96% at the noisiest level). My clustered keys flatter any index: on real embeddings, the same recall takes more clusters, and more time.
An external memory is less compact than weights: 1,024 bytes per fact here, or 8 to 64 bytes with compressed codes (Douze et al. 2024), against under five in the weights. But weights are read in full for every token. A lookup reads a few megabytes, only when a question needs it.

What a looked-up fact really costs
In retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al. 2020), what the index finds is pasted into the prompt. From then on it sits in the working memory and is reread for every generated token.



Figure 5. Computed for Llama 3.2 1B from the measurements above. Megabytes read per generated token, log scale. The search is paid once per question; retrieved passages on every token.


Each token of context costs this model 32 KB. Three passages of 300 tokens add 29 MB to every generated token, over five hundred times the search itself. That is still only 5% of the 620 MB of weights, and far less than a model ten times larger, which would read 6,200 MB per token to answer about 11 more points of questions (Section 6). A lookup is cheap only if what it brings back is short: a fact, not three pages.
That is why recent architectures put the lookup inside the model, where a fetched fact never becomes context. Meta’s memory layers read a few rows of a trainable table per token and beat dense models with more than twice the compute, most on factual questions (Berges et al. 2024). DeepSeek’s Engram adds a hashed n-gram table read in constant time (DeepSeek-AI 2026). Gemma 3n keeps per-layer embeddings on local storage (Google 2025).

title: Where Memory Lives
section: 7. What it means for small models and Fast AI
text:
7. What it means for small models and Fast AI



Figure 8. A proposal, my own. A small model reasons; a short working memory, an editable external memory and compiled habits surround it; a slow loop moves knowledge between them.



Keep in the weights what is used on every token: language, reasoning, tool use, the structure of a domain. Not the price list.
Keep the working memory short: summaries rather than transcripts, a compressed cache, a window.
Look up the long tail, and bring back little: the fact, not the page. Every row can be inspected, corrected and deleted.
Compile what repeats, as in Fast AI: a verified answer, a small tree or an adapter, checked before the model is called.
Consolidate slowly: what is looked up constantly may earn a place in a habit; what is wrong is deleted, in one line, not one training run.

Agent memory systems are building the top of this stack: MemGPT, now Letta, pages context like an operating system (Packer et al. 2023); Mem0 and A-MEM extract and link memories across sessions (Chhikara et al. 2025; Xu et al. 2025); Titans learns a memory at test time (Behrouz et al. 2024). A small model has the least room in its weights and the least bandwidth to spare, so it gains the most from putting each memory in the right place.

title: Where Memory Lives

title: Where Memory Lives
section: 9. What this experiment does not show
text:
9. What this experiment does not show

My facts are random. Real knowledge has structure a model can compress, so weights may do better than my networks.
My networks are tiny: two layers, at most 19,000 parameters.
My questions are synthetic. Real retrieval must embed a question first; it can miss, or find the fact and see the model ignore it.
Plain fine-tuning is the weakest editor. Better methods narrow the gap, but still edit weights that every fact shares.
NumPy is not a serving engine, which is why Figure 6 also gives the byte count.
Zipf is a model. A specialist’s questions may have a shorter tail, which argues for specialists.

title: Where Memory Lives
text:
10. Conclusion
We say a model knows something as if knowledge lived in one place. It lives in four, at four prices: dense weights read on every token, a working memory that grows with every token, a bulky but cheap and correctable lookup, and habits that cost almost nothing once built. Large models can afford to blur them. Small ones cannot, and that is their advantage. Keep in the weights what is used on every token, keep the working memory short, look up the long tail, compile what repeats.

Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.


Read next · An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle
The architecture these four memories fit into.


The views in this essay are my own and do not describe any product or plan of my employer.

title: Work Has Mass
text: An outsider’s view. I know Scrum from years of practice; SAFe I know only from its public framework, and practitioners will know where real trains differ. The physics is a metaphor, used on purpose; the numbers come from a toy model described in full. Figures are my own, made with figs.py. This essay follows the Agentic Coding series, which looked at the code; here I look at the organisation around it.

title: Work Has Mass
text:
The wrong debate
Conversations about AI and agile frameworks fall into two camps. One says AI makes Scrum and SAFe obsolete: if an agent builds a feature in an afternoon, why plan in two-week sprints, or in ten-week increments with a hundred people in a room? The other says nothing changes: AI is just a faster tool inside a good process.
Both camps look at production: how fast work is made. But the frameworks were never only about production. They are about how a group of people carries a growing body of work over time without losing control of it. What should change them is not what AI makes, but what it leaves behind. And the answer, I will argue, is not more framework. It is less.

title: Work Has Mass
text:
Every item has mass
Every item that enters the system stays for a while, and some stay for good: a story, a pull request, a feature, a test, a document, a dependency, an open decision, a backlog item someone will “get to later”. Each needs attention to keep: someone must understand it, maintain it, answer questions about it, or at least remember it is there.
I call that ongoing cost the item’s mass. Mass is not value. A small feature used by thousands can be light; a generated module nobody fully understands can be heavy.
In general relativity, mass curves spacetime: objects near a large mass follow curved paths, and time runs slower for them. That is a good picture of what accumulated work does to a team:

Paths bend. A new request is pulled toward the heavy parts of the system: the legacy module, the integration everyone depends on, the decision nobody has made.
Time slows near mass. The same change takes longer in a heavy system, because each step must account for more of what already exists.
There is a horizon. If mass keeps growing, all the team’s attention ends up carrying what exists. Requests still go in. Nothing comes out.




Figure 1. Schematic. Items sink the surface on which work moves. Left, the light system the frameworks were calibrated for: a shallow dip, and a request (amber, one dot per sprint) that crosses it almost straight. Right, the same system after AI has multiplied what the team produces: a deep well, and in the same nine sprints the request covers less ground and sinks toward the centre.


None of this is new. Lehman stated it as a law of software evolution: complexity grows unless work is spent to reduce it (Lehman 1980). Lean calls unfinished work inventory (Reinertsen 2009). Brooks showed that communication paths grow faster than headcount (Brooks 1975). What is new is the rate.

title: Work Has Mass
section: What AI changes: the cost of creating mass
text:
What AI changes: the cost of creating mass
AI makes producing an item much cheaper. It does not, or not yet, make carrying it much cheaper. Someone still has to decide whether a feature should exist, understand how it fits, own it when it breaks, and remember why it was built. As a balance:

\frac{dM}{dt} = \text{production} - \text{removal}, \qquad \text{capacity for new work} = H - k \cdot M,

where M is the mass of the system, H the team’s total attention and k the attention one unit of mass needs. Production has become cheap; removal was rarely planned at all. So M grows faster, and H - kM shrinks faster.
The smallest model I could build: a team has 100 hours of attention per sprint. The system starts with 250 items needing 0.1 hours each, so a quarter of the team already carries the past. A new item takes 6 hours to produce by hand or 1.5 with AI, plus 3 hours to absorb (review, decide, integrate). Whatever is left after carrying goes into new items, and every new item stays. These assumptions do most of the work; I return to them in the objections.



Figure 2. Toy model, one year of two-week sprints. Left: items in the system. Right: new items delivered per sprint. With AI, the team starts at twice the by-hand rate, but the mass it adds eats its capacity. With a mass budget (carrying capped at 35% of attention), the rate holds. Parameters are in the text and in figs.py.



By hand, the team delivers 8.3 items in the first sprint and 6.3 in the last; carrying grows from 25% to 44% of its attention.
With AI, it delivers 16.7 items in the first sprint, and every dashboard looks wonderful. By the end of the year it delivers 9.5, with 58% of its attention on carrying. In the second year the gain is almost gone: 5.3 items per sprint against 4.7 by hand.
With AI and a mass budget, whenever carrying would exceed 35% of attention, the team removes items (deletes code, retires features, closes backlog items) before adding new ones. It delivers 13 items per sprint, in the first year and the second.

Over the first year the budget buys little: 356 items against 332, about 7% more. What differs is where each team stands at the end: one delivers 13 items a sprint with a third of its attention on the past, the other 9.5 and falling, with almost 60% on the past. AI does not change the shape of the problem, only its speed. A system that took a decade to become heavy can now do it in a year, and our frameworks were tuned, implicitly, for the decade.

title: Work Has Mass
text:
Time dilation
Lead time depends on spare capacity. Queueing theory has known for sixty years that as load approaches capacity, waiting time does not grow steadily; it explodes (Kingman 1961; Little 1961). Mass eats spare capacity. Figure 3 adds one assumption to the model: requests arrive at a steady rate that needs 35% of the team.



Figure 3. Toy model. Lead time of a new request against the share of attention spent carrying existing mass. By hand, after a year, lead times nearly double; with AI and no budget, they are almost six times longer.


This is consistent with what teams report: we produce more than ever, and everything takes longer. In 2024, DORA found more AI adoption associated with slightly lower delivery throughput (about 1.5%) and stability (about 7.2%) (DORA, Google Cloud 2024). In 2025, throughput turned positive but stability stayed negative, and the authors’ explanation is close to this essay’s: change volume outruns the controls downstream, and teams in tightly coupled systems see little or no benefit (DORA, Google Cloud 2025). Experienced developers were even found slower with early-2025 tools in their own large, mature repositories (Becker et al. 2025). None of these studies measured mass, but all point the same way: the gain from faster making is smallest where there is most to carry.

title: Work Has Mass
text:
Measuring mass
Mass does not need to be precise to be seen. Two numbers are enough to start.

The carrying share. Tag every ticket, or every hour, as new or carry. Carry is everything spent on what already exists: support, incidents, upgrades, questions, reviews of changes that touch it. This is the x-axis of Figure 3.
The heaviest items. Once a quarter, attribute the carry hours to the items that caused them and list the top ten. Mass is very unequal; a few services, integrations or open decisions usually carry most of it. That list is where removal starts.

title: Work Has Mass
text:
A framework is mass too
The third law is the one I find most important. Every event, role, artifact, metric and tool in a framework is an item in the system, and costs attention every sprint whether or not it helps. Frameworks grow by addition, and almost nothing is removed. When AI makes the work heavier, a heavier process is the last thing the system needs. So I would apply one test to every element of Scrum and SAFe:

The mass test. Does this element remove or prevent more mass than it adds?




Figure 4. The mass test: my judgement, to be argued with. Each element of Scrum (circles) and SAFe (squares) is placed by the attention it costs every sprint and the mass it removes or prevents. Above the line, keep it; below, slim it or cut it. The arrow shows SAFe’s own move from a two-day PI Planning to a one-day PI Outcome Planning. Positions depend on the team; the test does not.


My placements matter less than the pattern. The parts that say no pass. The parts that count fail. A Sprint Goal, a Definition of Done, a review, an iteration reserved for removal: each decides what not to carry, and costs little. Estimating every item, refining a long backlog, synchronising a large train: each manages a quantity of work, and quantity is exactly what AI has made cheap. Some elements sit in between and can be slimmed rather than cut. PI Planning is the clearest case, and SAFe is already moving it: its AI-Native guidance replaces the two-day event with a one-day PI Outcome Planning, and folds the System Demo and Inspect and Adapt into a two-hour event each iteration (Scaled Agile, Inc. 2026). Applied honestly, the test does not reject either framework. It shrinks both to their core.

title: Work Has Mass
text:
Scrum: lighter, not looser
The Scrum Guide is already short: empiricism and lean thinking, a team of ten or fewer, a time-box of one month or less, five events and three commitments, the Product Goal, the Sprint Goal and the Definition of Done (Schwaber and Sutherland 2020). It says nothing about story points or velocity; those are common add-ons, and most of what makes Scrum heavy in practice lives in the add-ons.

Table 1. Scrum, read again with mass in mind. The middle column is my reading of the Scrum Guide and of common practice; the right column is my proposal.







Element
Calibrated for
In a heavier universe




Sprint
A rhythm to produce a usable increment
A rhythm to absorb one: decide, integrate, understand.


Sprint Goal
Focus for the sprint
Keep. The cheapest way to say no.


Definition of Done
The quality an increment must meet
Keep, and add: what it costs to carry, what was removed to make room.


Product Backlog
An ordered list, refined as needed
Short, with items that expire. AI can fill it without limit.


Sprint Review
Inspect the increment
Inspect the increment and the mass ledger (Figure 6).


Daily Scrum
Daily inspection toward the goal
Keep it short, or async for a small team.


Story points, velocity (add-ons, not in the Guide)
How much the team can make
Drop. With AI they measure mass added. Use lead time and the carrying share.


Team size
Ten or fewer, to keep communication manageable
The limit is the mass each person carries. Five people with AI can carry the mass of twenty.



The backlog needs evaporation. When writing a backlog item took effort, the effort was a filter. Now an AI can turn every meeting into ten well-written stories, and every story is a promise with mass. Untouched for three sprints, an item expires unless someone renews it. Black holes slowly evaporate. Backlogs should too.
What remains is Scrum at its core: a goal, a standard, a short list, a rhythm of inspection, and a ledger of what the team carries. Less framework than most teams run today, not more.

title: Work Has Mass
text:
SAFe: smaller trains, fewer layers
SAFe’s central structure is the Agile Release Train (ART), a long-lived team of agile teams, generally 50 to 125 people (Scaled Agile, Inc. 2023), that plans together every 8 to 12 weeks (Scaled Agile, Inc., n.d.-b). Work is ranked with Weighted Shortest Job First (WSJF): cost of delay divided by job size, an idea from product development flow (Reinertsen 2009).
SAFe already knows that existing work has weight. At each interval boundary, trains agree on a capacity allocation: the share of capacity for new features against enablers, technical debt and maintenance (Scaled Agile, Inc., n.d.-a). That is close to a mass budget, and trains that use it well are ahead. The difference is what is limited. A capacity allocation caps the effort spent on old work; a mass budget caps the old work itself, and forces removal when it grows.

WSJF stops discriminating
With AI, job sizes shrink, but unevenly: small features hit a floor, complex ones shrink less. The denominator loses its spread, and the ranking collapses toward cost of delay alone. And job size never measured what a feature costs to carry, which is now the larger part.



Figure 5. Illustrative, eight invented features, ranked by classic WSJF by hand, classic WSJF with AI, and WSJF with carrying cost. With AI the spread between best and worst score falls from 3.8× to 2.2×, and two features tie at the top. Carrying cost restores a 6.8× spread and moves features whose cost comes after delivery, like a chat assistant, down the list.


The fix is small: add the carrying cost to the denominator,

\text{WSJF}_{\text{mass}} = \frac{\text{cost of delay}}{\text{job size} + \text{carrying cost}},

where carrying cost is a relative estimate of the attention the feature will need in its first year. A chat assistant is quick to build and slow to carry, so it falls; a faster search adds almost nothing to carry, so it rises. And it is enough to score the top of the backlog: ranking features that will never be built is itself mass.


Smaller trains, fewer layers
50 to 125 people is a coordination limit, learned from teams who produced at human speed. But a train does not coordinate people; it coordinates what they produce and must keep consistent: interfaces, dependencies, shared data, shared decisions. If each person adds three times more mass, a train reaches that limit at about a third of the size.
The tempting answer is more structure. The mass test points the other way. Split trains by mass, long before 125 people, so that each carries less. Smaller trains need fewer sync meetings and fewer coordinating roles, and may need less of the structure above them. Planning shrinks with them: each team brings a mass budget next to its capacity, the board shows only the dependencies that cross teams, and the Innovation and Planning iteration becomes the home of removal. SAFe with AI should look less like a bigger SAFe and more like a few small, light trains, each with a clear budget of what it is allowed to carry.

title: Work Has Mass
text:
What I would actually do

Measure the carrying share and list the ten heaviest items.
Set a mass budget, and treat crossing it like a red build: stop adding, start removing.
Make removal a deliverable, shown at the Sprint Review and System Demo next to what was added.
Let items expire: backlog items, open questions, generated documents.
Price mass into priority: WSJF with carrying cost, for the top of the backlog only.
Size teams and trains by mass, not headcount.
Put the framework through the mass test, these seven proposals included.

That last point matters, because these are new practices and an essay against framework mass should not quietly add some. Each one replaces something heavier. The carrying share and lead time replace story points and velocity. Expiry replaces the refinement of a long backlog. The ledger replaces a status report, and is one chart in a review that already exists. The mass budget is a number in a planning event that already exists, not a new event. If one of them does not remove more than it adds in your team, drop it.



Figure 6. Illustrative. A mass ledger for one sprint, in hours per sprint of carrying cost: 51 added, 44 removed, net +7. This is the chart I would show at every Sprint Review, next to the increment.

title: Work Has Mass
text:
Objections
“This is technical debt, or Lean inventory, with a new name.” Partly. But a well-built feature that people use is neither debt nor inventory, and it must still be carried. Lean’s inventory is mostly unfinished work; the mass that grows fastest with AI is finished work. Lean also says to manage a system at its constraint (Goldratt and Cox 1984), and the constraint has moved from making to carrying.
“AI will carry the mass too.” In part, yes: agents already read code and summarise documents, which lowers k. If k falls as fast as production costs, this essay is wrong. I doubt it will, because the mass that matters most needs a person: accountability for a feature, the decision to keep or kill it, the customer who depends on it.
“Nobody gets promoted for deleting things.” True, and the strongest reason a mass budget may fail. Organisations reward what is added. That is why removal must be shown and counted at the same events as delivery, and why the ledger has two columns. What is not seen is not rewarded.
“The model is too simple.” It is: one team, constant parameters, items that never get lighter, and an AI that lowers the cost of making but not of carrying. The model shows the consequence of those assumptions, not their truth. If a better one shows mass levelling off on its own, I would like to see it.
“The physics is decoration.” Perhaps. But metaphors choose what we look at. Velocity made teams look at speed. Mass would make them look at what speed leaves behind.

title: Work Has Mass
text:
Conclusion
Scrum and SAFe are not wrong. Empiricism, short feedback loops, small teams, shared cadence and economic prioritisation are as useful with AI as without it. But both were calibrated in a universe where producing work was the hard part, and where mass grew slowly enough to be someone else’s problem later.
AI has changed the rate at which we create mass, not yet the rate at which we carry it. The reflex will be to add: more ceremonies to control more output, more roles to coordinate more teams, more layers to plan more work. That adds mass to a system already falling into its own well. The better answer is the opposite: measure the mass, budget it, price it, remove it as deliberately as we add, and then put the frameworks themselves on the scale.
Everything you make, you carry. In a heavier universe, start by carrying less framework.



Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.

title: Nothing From Outside, Everything From Inside
text: Continued in What Survives Comparison, which asks what happens with two observers instead of one.

title: Nothing From Outside, Everything From Inside
section: Two ideas that would not stay apart
text:
Two ideas that would not stay apart
In A Universe Without a Bottom I left two thoughts side by side. The first: maybe nothing creates everything. The second: maybe there are grains inside grains, with no final layer.
I treated them as separate questions. A few days later they started to look like one question. And the black hole formula, which I thought said there must be a floor, turned out to say something stranger.
I am still not a physicist. This is still curiosity. But I think I asked the earlier questions slightly wrong.

title: Nothing From Outside, Everything From Inside
text:
Nothing is not empty
In the last essay I called infinite temperature “the closest thing to nothing.” Every possibility equally likely. No preference, no structure.
That was half wrong. A state where every possibility is equally likely is not a state with zero information. It is the state with the most possibilities: maximum entropy. You cannot tell the possibilities apart, but they are all there.
This matters because of where the model points. For several years Susskind has argued that this exact system, at infinite temperature, describes de Sitter space: a universe with nothing in it except a horizon around the observer. An empty universe like this carries the largest entropy any region can have. Its horizon is covered with tiles, just like a black hole.
So the two images in my first essay may be the same image. “Nothing” and “a surface that knows everything” could be one thing, seen from different sides.

title: Nothing From Outside, Everything From Inside
text:
A universe with one state
Then I found a result that seemed to say the opposite.
Some universes are closed: travel in a straight line long enough and you come back to where you started. Our universe might be one of them. Over the last few years several groups calculated how many different states such a universe can be in, using the newest tools of quantum gravity. The answer kept coming out the same: one.
One state. Not a large number, not a small number. One. The whole universe, stars and galaxies included, would carry less information than a single coin toss. There is nothing to choose between, so there is nothing to know.
The physicists themselves did not like this. Our universe clearly has more than one possibility in it. I am writing this sentence and not another one. So what went wrong?

title: Nothing From Outside, Everything From Inside
text:
Someone has to be inside
The answer proposed by Harlow, Usatyuk and Zhao is simple to say. The calculation forgot the observer.
It described the universe as if from outside. But a closed universe has no outside. Nobody can stand there and look at it. The philosopher Thomas Nagel called the dream of perfectly objective knowledge the view from nowhere: the world seen from no particular place. Here the view from nowhere is not just hard to reach. It returns nothing.
So put an observer inside, treat the edge of that observer as a kind of boundary, and the many possibilities come back.
One warning, because the word is dangerous. “Observer” here does not mean a mind, a consciousness or a person. In these calculations an observer is any physical system with a limited number of internal states that can keep a record. A clock would do. A detector would do. Nothing mystical is happening. What changes is that there is now a reference point.
There is a catch, and I find it beautiful. How much of the universe the observer can describe depends on how much the observer can hold. A bigger observer, with more internal states, sees a richer and more accurate universe. A tiny one sees a blurry one.



Figure 1. How much the observer can hold. The same toy universe, described by observers that can keep more and more record. Each keeps only the largest-scale patterns it can afford; the tiny one sees a blur, the large one sees the filaments. The last panel is the whole toy universe, a view nobody inside actually has. Below: how faithful each description is, against the size of the observer. A toy, not a physics simulation; the code is in figs.py.


So the information in the universe is not simply “out there.” It exists between the universe and something inside it. This is close to an idea Carlo Rovelli proposed in 1996, relational quantum mechanics: physical properties are not owned by things, they exist only relative to other things. The new calculations do not prove this view. But they point the same way.

title: Nothing From Outside, Everything From Inside
text:
Two kinds of nothing
Now put the two results next to each other.

No observer: one state. Zero alternatives. Nothing to know.
One observer at the centre: a horizon full of tiles. Every alternative equally likely. Everything possible, nothing distinguishable.

Both look featureless. Both feel like “nothing.” But they are featureless for opposite reasons. The first has no possibilities. The second has all of them, and no way to tell them apart.



Figure 2. Two kinds of nothing. Left: a closed universe seen from nowhere, stars and galaxies included, counts as one state; all the probability sits on it. Right: put one observer at the centre and a horizon appears, covered with tiles; every pattern of tiles is equally likely, so every bar has the same height. Schematic, my own; the code is in figs.py.


Here is my step. Maybe these are not two different universes. Maybe they are the same universe, once without a reference point and once with one. Without one, the universe is nothing. With one, it is everything its horizon can hold.
This is less of a leap than I first thought. De Sitter space, taken as a whole, is itself a closed universe, so the one-state result should apply to it too. And in 2022, Chandrasekaran, Longo, Penington and Witten showed that the entropy of a de Sitter horizon only becomes well defined once an observer is included, and that empty de Sitter space is then the state of maximum entropy. As far as I know, nobody has put these results together in exactly this way. But the pieces fit.
Philosophers got here long before the equations. Hegel opened his Science of Logic (1812) with this very puzzle: pure being, with no determination at all, cannot be told apart from pure nothing. What sets things in motion, for Hegel, is becoming, the passage between the two. Two centuries later, physics seems to add one thing. What turns nothing into everything is a point of view.

title: Nothing From Outside, Everything From Inside
text:
Grains again
In the first essay I was stuck on a contradiction. History suggests the layers never end. The black hole formula says a region can hold only a limited amount of information, so it cannot hide infinite layers. There must be a floor.
Remember the 1987 bubble: a tiny pocket of dense energy that grows into a new universe. From outside it looks like a small black hole that disappears. From inside it is a whole cosmos.
Physicists have known for a long time that this is uncomfortable. A small black hole should hold only a little information. How can a whole universe fit inside? Wheeler called this kind of object a “bag of gold.”
The one-state result changes the question. At first, seen from outside, the bubble is a small black hole, and that black hole does carry some information on its surface. But the bubble then pinches off and becomes a separate closed universe. From that moment, with nothing of ours inside it, it counts as one state. It costs us almost nothing. From the inside, with its own observers, it is everything.



Figure 3. A bag of gold. Left: a slice of space drawn as a surface. Our universe sits above, falling into a small black hole; through the narrow neck (red), the horizon, it opens onto a large closed universe below. Right: the neck closes and the bubble pinches off. Counted from outside, it then carries one state. From inside, nothing has changed. Schematic, my own; the code is in figs.py.


And the same flip can repeat:

Inside that grain, a new bubble forms. To the grain, it counts as one state. To its own inhabitants, it is a cosmos.
Our universe might be a grain in someone else’s. To them, we would be one state. To us, we are everything.




Figure 4. Grains inside grains. Each panel zooms into one grain of the panel before it (circled in red). Seen from the grain around it, each one counts as a single state; seen by its own inhabitants, it is a whole universe, with grains of its own. Schematic, my own; the code is in figs.py.


Leibniz imagined something like this three centuries ago. In his Monadology (1714) he wrote that each portion of matter is like a garden full of plants, and that each branch of every plant is again such a garden. He also said that his ultimate units, the monads, “have no windows”: nothing comes in, nothing goes out. A grain that counts as one state from outside is a monad without windows.
Pascal, whose fear of infinite spaces I quoted last time, wrote in the same Pensées that we stand between two infinities, the infinitely large and the infinitely small, unable to see either end. He took this as a limit of human sight. Perhaps it is more than that. Perhaps each end is hidden by construction, from wherever anyone stands.
The contradiction disappears. Each level has a floor, but only for whoever counts from outside. The chain can go on forever because each grain is almost invisible to the one around it. The black hole formula does not forbid infinite layers. It only forbids seeing them.

title: Nothing From Outside, Everything From Inside
text:
Where information begins
I ended the first essay with “from nothing to nothing,” and the hope that the middle still matters. I would now say it differently.
Not from nothing to nothing. Nothing from outside, everything from inside, at every level, with no last level.
That makes my earlier ending more literal. If a universe has only one state until something inside it can keep a record, then the middle is not just where meaning lives. It is where information starts to exist. Not because anyone is conscious, but because something is somewhere.
This brings the question back to the usual subject of this blog. A large language model has a strangely similar shape. Before you ask it anything, it holds an enormous space of possible answers, all weighted, none chosen. Seen from outside, it is a horizon of possibilities with nothing in particular in it. An answer appears only when a question arrives from a particular place. Asking is not reading out something already written down. It is the moment the possibilities narrow into one.



Figure 5. An analogy, not physics. Left: a space of possible answers, drawn flat, before anyone asks: everything weighted, nothing chosen. Right: a question arrives from a particular place, and the possibilities narrow. The “spread” is the entropy of each picture, in bits. Schematic, my own; the code is in figs.py.


This is an analogy, not physics. I already took the first essay’s question to an image generator in Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary. But the lesson may be the same at both scales. Information is not stored somewhere, waiting. It happens at the boundary between a system and whatever stands inside it, or in front of it.
I started by believing the universe must be simple. Maybe it is. From outside, it is as simple as anything can be: one state. The complexity is a view from inside. And we are inside.

title: Nothing From Outside, Everything From Inside
text:
What I am not claiming

The one-state result comes mostly from simplified models, often with gravity in two dimensions. Physicists find it fairly convincing, but it is not settled for our universe.
Linking it to the de Sitter results is my own reading. As far as I know, none of the papers below states it this way.
Whether a 1987-style bubble really becomes a closed universe in the sense of these calculations is an open question.
The idea that the nesting never ends is speculation, not a result.
Hegel, Leibniz, Pascal and the comparison with AI are echoes, not evidence. They show the idea is old, not that it is true.


Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.

title: Intent Is the Source
text:
Agentic Coding · Part 3 of 5 · Read the whole series
Abstract. Each generation of programming has turned what people used to write into something the machine generates: machine code into the output of assemblers, assembly into the output of compilers, boilerplate into the output of frameworks. I argue that agentic coding, in which a language model plans, edits, runs and repairs code inside a loop, is the next step on this ladder, and a larger one than it looks. The thesis is that the agentic loop is both the next IDE and the next programming language. I define a program as a tuple P = (I, T, K, \Gamma) of intent, executable checks, context and tools, and the agent as a stochastic compiler that is correct only up to the checks. From this definition follow four arguments (historical, structural, economic, empirical), one central consequence (the precision of the new language is the strength of its checks), and four predictions that can be measured within a few years. I end with the strongest objections, including Dijkstra’s, and the evidence that currently cuts against me.

title: Intent Is the Source
text:
1. Introduction
Programming languages are usually described by their syntax and semantics. A more useful description, for the argument here, is what a person has to write and what the machine produces from it. By that measure, the history of programming is a ladder. On each rung, people stopped writing one thing and started writing something more abstract, while the old thing kept existing as output.



Figure 1. Schematic. Each generation of programming turned what people used to write into what the step above generates. The examples are illustrative.


Since code-generating language models appeared (Chen et al. 2021), the obvious question has been whether they are a better autocomplete or something else. Andrej Karpathy framed neural networks as “Software 2.0” (Karpathy 2017) and, more recently, described prompting models in English as a new kind of programming (Karpathy 2025). I take a narrower and more testable position. I do not claim that English replaces programming languages. I claim that the unit a person writes is changing from code to a bundle of intent and checks, and that the environment a person works in is changing from an editor to a loop. If both hold, then the agentic loop is, in the plain historical sense, the next language and the next IDE.

title: Intent Is the Source
text:
2. Background
The ladder. When FORTRAN appeared in 1957, its designers faced deep scepticism that machine-generated code could approach hand-written assembly; much of their effort went into the optimiser, precisely to win that argument (Backus 1978). They won, and the pattern repeated with every later level of abstraction.
Natural language as code. The idea of programming in English is old. Jean Sammet discussed it in 1966 (Sammet 1966); Edsger Dijkstra called it foolish in the late 1970s, arguing that the precision of formal notation is a feature, not a burden (Dijkstra, n.d.). Program synthesis research pursued the goal from specifications and examples for decades (Gulwani et al. 2017), with success in narrow domains.
Agents that code. Language models trained on code reached usable accuracy on small functions in 2021 (Chen et al. 2021). Since then, agents that read a repository, edit files, run tests and iterate have been evaluated on real GitHub issues (Jimenez et al. 2024; Yang et al. 2024). The productivity evidence is mixed: a controlled experiment found developers 55.8% faster on a small, well-specified task with an AI pair programmer (Peng et al. 2023), while a randomised study of experienced open-source developers on their own mature repositories found them 19% slower with early-2025 tools (Becker et al. 2025).

title: Intent Is the Source
text:
3. A minimal definition
I define a program, in the agentic sense, as a tuple

P = (I,\; T,\; K,\; \Gamma),

where I is the intent, what is wanted, stated in words and examples; T is a set of executable checks (tests, types, properties, linters) that a candidate implementation must pass; K is the context, the repository and its conventions; and \Gamma is the set of tools and interfaces the agent may use, described as data in the sense of The Interface Is Data.
An agent A maps a program to code, c = A(P). A classical compiler is deterministic and preserves meaning by construction. An agent does neither. It is a stochastic compiler: its output can vary between runs, and it is correct only in the weak sense that

T(c) = \text{pass}.

Call the specification gap of P the set of behaviours that pass T but are not what I meant. The whole discipline of the new language is to make this gap small: by sharpening I, by strengthening T, and by having a person review what remains.



Figure 2. Schematic. The agent as a stochastic compiler. The program is the tuple of intent, checks, context and tools. The agent produces code, which is checked automatically and then reviewed by a person. Failed checks send the agent back; review refines the intent and strengthens the checks.


Under this definition, the concepts of the familiar toolchain map onto new ones.

Table 1. The toolchain, translated. My own mapping.


Today
In the agentic loop




Source file
Intent, examples and checks: (I, T)


Compiler
Agent: c = A(P), stochastic


Type checker
Tests, types and properties: T(c)


Standard library
Tools and interfaces: \Gamma


Build configuration
Repository context and conventions: K


Debugger
Decision log and execution trace of the agent


Code review
Review of intent first, then of the diff


Editor
Plan, diff and checks panes; typing as fallback

title: Intent Is the Source
text:
4. Four arguments
4.1 Historical. Every previous rung of the ladder was resisted on the grounds that generated output was slower, less precise or less trustworthy than what experts wrote by hand (Backus 1978). Each time, the generated output improved, the cost of writing by hand stayed the same, and the line crossed. Nothing in the current situation suggests the pattern has stopped; the objections raised today are the same three.
4.2 Structural. Brooks distinguished the essential complexity of software, deciding precisely what it must do, from its accidental complexity, the effort of expressing that decision in a particular language and toolset (Brooks 1987). Under the definition above, a person writes I and T, which carry the essential complexity, and the agent handles the expression, which is accidental. This is the division of labour every abstraction has aimed for, achieved at a higher level than before. Tests, long promoted as a design discipline (Beck 2002), become the main way to state that essential part.
4.3 Economic. The cost of producing a correct change has three parts: writing it, checking it, and understanding it later. Agentic coding drives the first towards zero and leaves the other two. A rational team will therefore spend its people where the cost remains, on intent, checks and review, which is exactly the shift from editor to loop that the thesis predicts. The IDE follows the work: when typing is no longer the bottleneck, an environment organised around typing is the wrong shape.
4.4 Empirical. Agents now resolve a meaningful share of real repository issues under controlled evaluation (Jimenez et al. 2024; Yang et al. 2024), a task that requires reading context, editing several files and passing existing tests: the full loop of Figure 2, not autocomplete. The negative result of Becker et al. (2025) is important and I return to it in §6, but it measures an early tool generation, on large mature repositories, with developers who had little experience of the new way of working. That is close to measuring FORTRAN in 1957 with assembly experts.

title: Intent Is the Source
text:
5. Predictions
A position paper should be falsifiable. If the thesis is right, the following should be observed in professional software over the next few years; if they are not, it is wrong.

H1. Authorship shifts. The share of merged changes whose code was primarily produced by an agent keeps rising in professional repositories, measurable from commit metadata and tool logs.
H2. Checks grow relative to code. In human-written lines, the ratio of tests, types and specifications to implementation rises.
H3. Review becomes the main human cost. Time spent reviewing and specifying exceeds time spent writing code, in the same teams that adopt agents.
H4. Gains follow the strength of checks. Productivity gains from agents are larger where T is strong (well-tested code with clear conventions) than where it is weak, other things equal. This is the most direct test of claim 3.

title: Intent Is the Source
text:
6. Objections
Natural language is too imprecise (Dijkstra). This is right, and it is the most important objection. But the program in §3 is not prose alone. Its precision lives in T, in K and in review, as it always has in teams where a person states a need and an engineer implements it. The objection becomes a design rule: wherever precision matters, state it as a check, not as a sentence.
A stochastic compiler cannot be trusted. Deterministic compilers can be trusted because their meaning-preservation can be argued once. A stochastic compiler cannot; it must be checked every time. This raises the value of T and of review, and it means that for code where checks are weak and errors are costly, the old way should remain. The thesis predicts a shift in the default, not the end of hand-written code.
Developers are slower, not faster (Becker et al. 2025). If replications on strong-check repositories, with experienced users of current tools, continue to find slowdowns, H4 fails and so does much of this paper. I consider this the most likely way for me to be wrong.
Code is still the artefact that runs. Yes, as assembly still runs. The thesis does not say code disappears; it says it stops being the thing people mainly write. Like assembly, it remains the layer that can always be read, and to which the machine is held.
Literate programming tried this. Knuth argued that programs should be written for people first (Knuth 1984). Literate programming kept the person as the author of the code. The difference here is that the person is the author of the intent and the checks, and the code is derived.

title: Intent Is the Source
text:
7. Conclusion
Every generation of programmers was told that the next level of abstraction was a toy, and each time the toy became the language. I have argued, on purpose without hedging, that the agentic loop is the next such level: the source becomes intent plus checks, the compiler becomes a stochastic agent held to those checks, and the IDE becomes a place to steer and review. The definition makes one consequence precise. The new language is exactly as rigorous as its checks, so the craft of programming does not disappear; it moves into specification, testing and judgement. Four predictions make the claim testable. I expect to be partly wrong. I would rather be wrong in a way that can be measured.

Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.


Read next · The Interface Is Data How MCP and the agentic loop change what we call an API.
